EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN – HOOKWORM ERADICATION AND SOUTHERN DEVELOPMENT  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1. Identification Strategy  
Chosen design: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study extension (Sun & Abraham 2020) plus an Instrumental-Variables (IV) first stage to purge remaining endogeneity in infection rates.

Why DID/event study?  
• The Rockefeller Sanitary Commission (RSC) rolled out mobile dispensaries in a staggered, county-by-county fashion between 1909-1915.  
• We observe repeated county-level outcomes (1910–1950) before and after the intervention.  
• There are many never-treated or late-treated counties that can serve as contemporaneous controls.  

Why add an IV?  
Even within treated counties, the decline in infection is heterogeneous (e.g., related to local take-up, soil type).  To map the biological shock (infection drop) to outcomes we instrument the post-1909 change in hookworm prevalence with the interaction of (i) baseline 1910 infection rate and (ii) an indicator for RSC presence in that year.  

Combined estimator:  
(1) Event-study DID → intent-to-treat (ITT) effect of the public health campaign.  
(2) 2SLS where ∆Hookworm ct is instrumented by BaselineInfection c × Treated ct → causal effect of an actual percentage-point reduction in infection.

2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment variable  
ITT: Treated ct = 1 in county c and year t ≥ first year an RSC dispensary operated in c, 0 otherwise.  
Continuous treatment (2SLS): ∆Hookworm ct = (% infected) ct – (% infected) c,1910.

Control group  
• Counties not yet visited by the RSC in year t (“future-treated”) plus counties that were never visited.  
• Both groups are pooled but we allow for state-by-year fixed effects to net out statewide shocks.

Treatment timing  
Event time τ = t – StartYear c ; τ = 0 in first year of treatment, τ<0 pre-period, τ>0 post.

No running variable → not an RDD.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of RSC activity, treated and comparison counties would have evolved similarly.  Plausibility: RSC targeted high-infection but not necessarily high-growth counties; we add county FE, state-year FE, and control for pre-1909 trends.  

A2. No anticipatory behavior: Counties did not change schooling or farming decisions prior to knowing exact RSC arrival.  RSC scheduling was often logistical (rail access), supporting plausibility.  

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no cross-county contagion): Limited spillovers because hookworm is transmitted by local soil; we still test for spatial spillovers using distance-band exclusions.  

A4. First-stage relevance (IV): The interaction BaselineInfection c × Treated ct strongly predicts infection decline post-treatment – documented by medical inspections.  

4. Threats to Identification & Remedies  

T1. Non-parallel pre-trends (most serious)  
 • Graphical and formal event-study pre-coefficients.  
 • Include county-specific linear trends.  
 • Re-weight controls via synthetic-control DID (Arkhangelsky et al. 2021).

T2. Migration responses  
 • Construct net-migration rates from Census microdata; include as outcome and control; show results are similar after excluding high in-migration counties.

T3. Other contemporaneous reforms (e.g., compulsory schooling laws)  
 • Control for year × state education legislation dummies.  
 • Conduct triple-differences: compare to low-hookworm‐risk counties in contiguous states.

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# Load libraries
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast fixed-effects DID
library(fastDummies) # for dummy creation
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Data loading
dt <- fread("county_hookworm_panel_1910_1950.csv")   # one row per county-year

# 2. Variable construction
# Treatment timing
dt[, treat_year := min(year[RSC_visit == 1]), by = county_id]
dt[, ever_treated := !is.infinite(treat_year)]
dt[, treated := as.integer(year >= treat_year & ever_treated == TRUE)]

# Event time
dt[, event_time := ifelse(ever_treated, year - treat_year, NA_integer_)]
dt <- dt[event_time > -11 & event_time < 31]   # keep window (-10, +30)

# Baseline infection (1910)
dt[, base_inf := infection_rate[year == 1910], by = county_id]
dt[, instrument := base_inf * treated]         # IV for 2SLS

# 3. Main DID ITT specification
itt_mod <- feols(outcome_income ~ treated | county_id + state_year, 
                 data = dt, cluster = ~state)

# 4. Event-study (Sun & Abraham)
es_mod <- feols(outcome_income ~ sunab(treat_year, year, ref.p = -1) | 
                county_id + state_year, data = dt, cluster = ~state)

# 5. 2SLS using infection decline
ivs_mod <- feols(outcome_income ~ f(infection_rate, 1) | 
                 county_id + state_year | infection_rate ~ instrument, 
                 data = dt, cluster = ~state)

# 6. Robustness: exclude counties within 50km of treated counties (spillover test)
dt[, near_treated := min(dist_km[ever_treated == TRUE]), by = county_id]
robust_dt <- dt[near_treated > 50]
robust_mod <- feols(outcome_income ~ treated | county_id + state_year, 
                    data = robust_dt, cluster = ~state)

# 7. Output
etable(itt_mod, ivs_mod, robust_mod, tex = FALSE)
```

6. Expected Results  

Theory (health → productivity & schooling) predicts positive effects.  
• Income per capita: +12 – 20 % after 20 years (≈0.10–0.18 log points).  
• School enrollment: +5 ppt by 1920.  
• Literacy: +3–4 ppt by 1930.  
Largest gains in child-intensive outcomes early, income later.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  

C1: Clear treatment timing and variation ……………… 1  
C2: Parallel pre-trends demonstrated ………………… 1 (to be verified)  
C3: No simultaneous shocks correlated with treatment … 0.5  
C4: No spillovers/contamination ………………………… 0.5  
C5: Correct standard-error clustering/inference ……… 1  
Total = 4 / 5 (credible, but must scrutinize pre-trends & spillovers).
